We are also urged to refrain from adopting the rules proposed in the Interim Report, because they will accelerate the decay of central cities. The rules we are adopting herein merely reflect certain developments that have occurred since the mid-1940's. We do not believe it advisable to attempt to deal with the urban problems presently affecting certain cities through our interpretation and application of the provisions of the Interstate Commerce Act. These problems are better met head-on. There are also assertions that commercial zone expansion will stimulate new entrants into the motor carrier industry leading to increased traffic congestion. Potential problems of this nature are dealt with in the environmental impact statement attached hereto as Appendix C. We emphasize here that we are discussing the <u>primary</u> impact on interstate commerce of the section 203(b)(8) exemption. Since every municipality has a commercial zone and certain interstate shipments can come into a commercial zone and retain their interstate character through a subsequent but "non-continuous" movement in local carriage, it is conceivable that in certain situations the commercial zone exemption is relevant to local transportation at cities neither near nor straddling a State line. In real economic terms, however, the impact of 203(b)(8) in this context is minimal.
Local planners are considering and experimenting with a number of solutions to this problem in those cities where it is acute. See, Verbit, The Urban Transportation Problem, 124 U. PENN. L.R. 368, 440-41 (1975).
